conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode; 'session' means one trading day of intraday bars; standard Brooks setups referenced only by name (wedge, high 1, double top/bottom bear flag, consecutive climaxes, reversal bar) are primitives from earlier chapters and are not redefined here

candidates.name: OpeningRangeHeightVsAverageDailyRange
candidates.quote: Since the opening range was greater than about 30 percent of the average range of recent days, the opening range was not a good breakout mode setup.
candidates.description: Primitive with state: track the current session's opening-range high/low over its first N bars, and the average of the last M completed sessions' full-day range (high-low).
candidates.pseudocode: newSession = Date(0) != Date(1); if (newSession) { if (haveOpeningRange) pushDailyRange(sessionHigh - sessionLow); sessionHigh = high[0]; sessionLow = low[0]; barsIntoSession = 0; openingRangeSet = false } else { barsIntoSession++; sessionHigh = max(sessionHigh, high[0]); sessionLow = min(sessionLow, low[0]) } if (!openingRangeSet && barsIntoSession == openingRangeBars) { openingRangeHigh = sessionHigh; openingRangeLow = sessionLow; openingRangeHeight = openingRangeHigh - openingRangeLow; openingRangeSet = true } avgDailyRange = average(lastNDailyRanges, dayLookback)

complexity.reason: needs session-boundary detection and a rolling multi-day range history built from intraday bars

notes: Same primitive as T22-01/T23-01, redefined per this chapter's scope; the dedup pass should merge them.

candidates.name: LargeOpeningRangeWeakensBreakoutOdds
candidates.quote: Since the opening range was greater than about 30 percent of the average range of recent days, the opening range was not a good breakout mode setup. The likelihood of a strong, relentless trend after a bull breakout was less.
candidates.description: Filter: the opening-range height already exceeds a fraction of the recent average daily range, so a later breakout is unlikely to become a strong, relentless (trend-from-open or small-pullback) trend; if a trend does form it is more likely to be a weaker variant such as a trending trading range day.

complexity.reason: single comparison once T24-01's aggregates are available

notes: The mirror image of T22-02/T23-02's small-opening-range breakout-mode filters.

candidates.name: PartialProfitWhenTrendUnclear
candidates.quote: Since a strong bull trend was unlikely, bulls should take at least half off after about two to four points' profit.
candidates.description: Exit: when the large-opening-range filter (T24-02) is active, scale out part of a with-trend position at a modest fixed/ATR profit target instead of holding for a full swing, since a strong relentless trend is less likely that day.
candidates.pseudocode: largeOpeningRangeSession && ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && ctx.OpenPositionProfit() >= partialTargetAtr * atr * bigPointValue
candidates.book_order_type: limit order for a partial exit

complexity.reason: an ATR-scaled profit test gated on the regime filter

candidates.name: RunawaySpikeAlwaysInFlipAnytime
candidates.quote: The market can enter a runaway trend mode where it trends relentlessly with only minor pullbacks. There are large trend bars with little overlap and mostly small tails. This is a breakout and a clear always-in flip. You must enter quickly, even if the new trend looks climactic and overdone.
candidates.description: Filter: a multi-bar run of large trend bars with little overlap and small tails, occurring at any point in the session (not just the open), flips the always-in direction and licenses aggressive with-trend entries even though the move already looks extended.
candidates.pseudocode: for k in 0..spikeBars-1: largeTrendBar[k] (same direction) && overlapFrac[k] <= maxOverlap; all true -> alwaysIn = direction, ignoreExtendedLookGuard = true
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter, paired with an at-the-market or breakout entry)

complexity.reason: reuses the spike/overlap window-loop tests, just without an opening-of-session restriction

notes: Same underlying primitive as the spike-and-channel chapter's BullSpike; this entry is distinguished only by not requiring it to happen near the open.

candidates.name: CountertrendSpikeWithinPullbackWarnsReversal
candidates.quote: There is almost always at least one countertrend spike before the channel begins, so whenever you see a pullback that has a strong countertrend spike, be aware that the trend might be reversing.
candidates.description: Filter: while in an established trend, a pullback against it contains its own multi-bar spike (large trend bars against the prevailing direction with little overlap); this warns that the pullback may grow into a full trend reversal rather than a normal correction.
candidates.pseudocode: prevailingTrend == 1 /* bull */ && for k in 0..counterSpikeBars-1: largeBearTrendBar[k] && overlapFrac[k] <= maxOverlap; all true -> reversalWarning = true

complexity.reason: needs a notion of the prevailing trend plus a spike test applied specifically to the pullback leg

candidates.name: PullbackExceedsPriorLegHeightBecomesReversal
candidates.quote: By the end of the day, the pullback can grow larger than the bear trend that preceded it, and the day could become a bull reversal bar on the daily chart.
candidates.description: Filter: once a warned pullback's move (from the trend extreme) exceeds the height of the trend leg that preceded it, treat the session as having flipped into an opposite trend rather than a pullback -- restrict further entries to the new (pullback) direction.

complexity.reason: a size comparison against a remembered leg height

candidates.name: RestrictToPullbackDirectionOnCountertrendSpike
candidates.quote: If you recognize this behavior early, you should restrict your trading to buying only, because you will lose money on shorts as you desperately hope that the bear trend from the first hour resumes.
candidates.description: Filter: once T24-06 fires, block entries in the original trend direction for the rest of the session and trade only in the new (pullback) direction.

complexity.reason: a direct gate on the state produced by T24-06

candidates.name: PriorDayLateReversalFollowThroughBias
candidates.quote: If the reversal starts in the last couple of hours and is strong, it will usually have follow-through on the next day and often the next several days.
candidates.description: Filter: if the prior session closed with a strong reversal that began in its final N hours (the session's close-to-open-of-that-window move exceeds a size threshold, opposite to the direction the session had been trending before that window), bias today's with-trend entries toward that same (reversal) direction.
candidates.pseudocode: priorSessionHadLateReversal && abs(priorSessionClose - priorSessionPriceAtLateWindowStart) >= reversalSizeAtr * atr -> preferDirectionBias = priorReversalDirection
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context bias carried across the session boundary)

complexity.reason: needs one session's outcome remembered and classified, then applied as a bias on the next session

candidates.name: WedgeCorrectionMinimumBarCount
candidates.quote: After a large wedge bottom, the market usually has at least a two-legged rally that tests the top of the wedge...and the number of bars in the correction is usually at least a third or so of the number of bars in the wedge.
candidates.description: Filter/context: after a wedge-bottom reversal, treat the correction as still incomplete (likely to need a further, larger leg, and a full reversal reading as premature) until the rally's bar count reaches a fraction of the wedge's own bar count.

complexity.reason: requires wedge detection (three-push, swing pivots) plus a bar-count ratio test

candidates.name: WedgeFailureMeasuredMoveDownWithExtensionLeg
candidates.quote: When there is a wedge reversal, it is usually safer to buy after a higher low...Bars 11, 13, and 14 formed a wedge bull flag, but the market broke to the downside instead of reversing up. When that happens, the market usually falls to about a measured move down from the top to the bottom of the wedge...When that happens, there is usually another leg down after a pullback.
candidates.description: Exit/target: when a bull wedge flag breaks down instead of reversing up, project a measured-move-down target (wedge top minus wedge height) from the breakdown point; if price exceeds that target, expect an additional leg down after the next pullback rather than treating the first target as final.
candidates.pseudocode: wedgeBrokeDown && target1 = wedgeBreakdownPoint - (wedgeTop - wedgeBottom); if (low[0] <= target1) expectAdditionalLegDown = true

complexity.reason: wedge detection plus measured-move projection and a second-leg expectation flag

candidates.name: NoPullbackAfterFirstLegSignOfStrength
candidates.quote: Since the bears could not generate much of a downside breakout in the channel...no clear two-legged move ever developed. This absence of any clear pullback after a first leg up was a sign of strength by the bulls.
candidates.description: Filter: after a first leg of a new move completes, if no bar closes back through a minimum retracement fraction of that leg before a new extreme is made, treat the lack of a qualifying pullback itself as a sign of strength and favor with-trend entries over waiting for a 'proper' pullback.
candidates.pseudocode: firstLegHigh reached; noQualifyingPullback = true; for each bar since: if (close[0] <= firstLegHigh - minRetraceFraction * firstLegHeight) noQualifyingPullback = false; if (high[0] > firstLegHigh && noQualifyingPullback) signOfStrength = true

complexity.reason: a running retracement check against a remembered leg high, once the leg is identified

candidates.name: SmallerTimeframeEntriesInRunawayTrend
candidates.quote: In a runaway bull trend, there are more chances to buy on the 3 minute chart than on the 5 minute chart.
candidates.description: Research idea: in a confirmed runaway trend, running entry logic on a faster secondary bar series (e.g. 3-minute alongside a 5-minute primary) surfaces additional with-trend setups the slower series misses.
candidates.pseudocode: n/a - requires evaluating the same entry primitives against a second, faster bar series while the runaway-trend flag is set

complexity.reason: needs multi-timeframe bar access, which is an engine/design decision, not a single-series bar test

chapter_summary: Chapter 24 is short: a reversal day trends one way and then reverses into the close, and most reversal days begin as trending trading range days. Its minable content is mostly context filters -- a runaway spike can flip always-in at any time of day (not just the open), a countertrend spike inside a pullback warns the pullback may become a full reversal, an oversized opening range predicts a weaker breakout, a strong late-day reversal tends to carry over to the next session, and the absence of an expected pullback is itself read as trend strength -- plus wedge-specific correction-length and failed-wedge measured-move targets. Consecutive-climax and daily-bar reversal-signal material here duplicates chapters 21/22; not re-mined.
